analysis.one_liner: Requires big freight railroads to give their workers at least seven days of paid sick leave a year.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a House floor vote and died when the 118th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the large Class I freight railroads to give every employee at least seven paid sick days a year, usable for the worker's own illness, a doctor's visit, caring for family, or dealing with domestic violence. The days would carry over year to year, be paid at the worker's regular wage, and railroads could not discipline or fire someone for using them. It also cut off federal approval of a railroad's safety plan if the railroad did not comply. The bill was introduced in May 2023 and referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Freight rail workers — conductors, engineers, and other railroad employees — gain guaranteed paid sick days they can take without hunting for a replacement worker or accruing attendance penalties. Their families gain when a worker can stay home to care for a sick child or handle a personal crisis. Travelers and communities near rail lines also benefit indirectly, since rested, healthy crews are tied to safer operations.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Freight rail workers and their families

how_it_helps.text: Each Class I railroad would have to provide employees at least 7 days of paid sick leave per calendar year, and vacation, personal days, holidays, and other accrued or unpaid leave would not count toward that minimum.

Workers could use the leave for their own illness or medical care, to care for a child, parent, spouse, domestic partner, or chosen family member, and for absences related to domestic violence, sexual assault, or stalking.

Sick leave would be paid at the employee's regular hourly wage rate, unused days would carry over to the next year, and carriers could not make leave use contingent on the employee finding a replacement to cover the missed work.

Railroads would be barred from firing, suspending, laying off, demoting, disciplining — including assigning attendance points or demerits — or denying promotion or training to an employee because they requested or used paid sick leave.

The bill included an enforcement lever: the Transportation Department could not approve a railroad's safety risk reduction program plan if the carrier had not complied with the sick leave requirements.
The 7-day minimum would apply regardless of what collective bargaining agreements say, with additional days negotiable under the Railway Labor Act.

analysis.who_pays: The Class I freight railroads — companies like the major national freight carriers — would bear the direct cost of paid sick leave, including paying the full regular wage (with its compensation elements) for days taken. Carriers could face scheduling costs from covering absences without requiring employees to find substitutes. Some carriers might pass costs into freight rates, which would eventually show up in prices of shipped goods.

drawbacks.text: The mandate imposes a real cost on the railroads: seven paid days per worker at the regular wage, including all compensation elements, plus the cost of covering absences without a replacement-worker rule, which falls directly on carrier operations.

Tying approval of federally required safety risk reduction plans to sick leave compliance mixes a labor benefit into a safety program, so a carrier could lose safety-plan approval over a labor dispute — a link an honest opponent would call an aggressive enforcement tool rather than a neutral safety measure.

The bill set a 7-day advance notice requirement for foreseeable leave, which could complicate crew scheduling for railroads that run around-the-clock operations, though it allowed 'as soon as practicable' requests for unforeseeable needs.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit to workers is concrete and meaningful: rail workers are among the few workforces with no guaranteed sick days, and the bill targeted the exact practices — needing a replacement and attendance-point discipline — that make taking a sick day risky. The costs fall on a small set of very profitable Class I railroads and, at most indirectly, on shipping prices. The main design quibble is bolting the enforcement onto the safety-plan approval process, but that is a mechanism choice, not a flaw that undermines the core benefit. On balance the help to workers outweighs the cost.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which passed it to a rail subcommittee and then never brought it up, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Payne Jr. introduced the bill on May 11, 2023, joined by 36 original cosponsors.
The same day it was introduced, the House referred it to the Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure.
The next day, May 12, 2023, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials.

No markup, committee vote, floor vote, or further action followed; the bill's action history ends with the subcommittee referral, and the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025 without the bill moving.
All 53 cosponsors the bill accumulated were House Democrats; no Republicans signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The Class I freight railroads are better off, since they avoided a federal mandate to provide seven paid sick days and the enforcement mechanism tying safety-plan approval to compliance. Rail workers got nothing: their sick leave remained whatever their employer or bargaining agreements provided.

for.name: Rep. Donald Payne Jr.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; none of them chaired a committee that advanced it.

against.role: Chair, House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee

against.name: Class I freight railroads
against.role: BNSF, Union Pacific, CSX, Norfolk Southern and other major carriers
against.what_they_did: Opposed federal mandates for paid sick leave, arguing sick days should be set through collective bargaining; the industry fought similar leave provisions during the 2022 national rail contract dispute.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — the sponsor and all 53 cosponsors were House Democrats, with no Republican cosponsors — and the bill died in a committee controlled by Republicans without any vote ever being taken.

industries.note: The bill would have required these carriers to pay seven sick days per worker at full regular wage and to drop replacement-worker and attendance-point rules around sick leave — a direct cost to them and a direct benefit to their workers. By killing the bill, the carriers kept their existing leave practices in place.

industries.industry: Rail labor unions and freight rail workers
industries.note: Guaranteed paid sick leave was a top demand of rail unions, which secured no paid sick days in the 2022 national contract Congress imposed. The bill would have delivered it by statute, with additional days left to bargaining.
